chapters.title: Chapter 2: Government-Backed and Fixed Return Options

lessons.title: Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana and Senior Citizens Savings Scheme

children.text: Most 80C options are open to everyone. These two are not. Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana is only for parents of a young daughter, and the Senior Citizens Savings Scheme is only for people at or near retirement. That exclusivity is exactly why they pay the highest rates among government small savings schemes. If you, or your parents, fall into either group, these deserve a hard look before anything else.

children.text: SSY is a savings account in your daughter's name, opened and operated by a parent or guardian until she turns 18. It works like a supercharged PPF for a girl's education and marriage: EEE tax status, a higher rate, and a long, protected tenure. The parent who deposits claims the deduction under Section 123 (80C) on the old regime.

cells: Parent or legal guardian of a girl below 10 years of age, resident in India
One per girl, maximum two per family (three if the second birth is twins or triplets)
₹250 to ₹1,50,000 per financial year, for the first 15 years only
21 years from the date of opening
Up to 50% of the balance at the end of the previous financial year, after the girl turns 18 or passes Class 10, for education
On marriage after age 18, death of the girl, life-threatening illness, or death of the guardian
Account becomes a default account; revive by paying ₹250 per missed year plus ₹50 penalty per year
EEE: deposit deductible on the old regime, interest and maturity tax-free under both regimes

body.caption: 15 years of deposits at the start of each year, then 6 more years of growth with no deposits. At ₹1,50,000 a year and a constant 8.2%, this is about ₹71.82 lakh.

body.label: Tax-free interest earned over 21 years
body.context: On ₹22.5 lakh deposited, if the rate stays at 8.2%. Nearly 69% of the maturity value is interest, and none of it is taxed.

body.text: Unlike NSC or SCSS, the SSY rate is not locked when you open the account. It changes whenever the government resets small savings rates, which happens quarterly. SSY paid 9.2% in 2015-16 and dropped to 7.6% from April 2020 before rising back to 8.2%. The ₹71.82 lakh figure is an illustration, not a promise.

body.title: Eligibility Check
body.question: Which of these families can open a new SSY account in September 2026?
options: The Mehtas in Surat, for their 11-year-old daughter
The Khans in Hyderabad, for their third daughter, born as a single birth
The Rajputs in Jaipur, for their 4-year-old daughter, their only child
The D'Souzas, NRIs living in Dubai, for their 2-year-old daughter
body.explanation: The girl must be below 10, so the Mehtas are too late. A third account is allowed only when the second birth is twins or triplets, which rules out the Khans. SSY is for residents, which rules out the D'Souzas. The Rajputs' 4-year-old qualifies.

body.title: Your Turn: The Education Withdrawal
body.prompt: Pallavi turns 18 in 2043 and gets admission to an engineering college. Her SSY balance was ₹38,40,000 at the end of the previous financial year. What is the maximum partial withdrawal allowed for her education?
body.explanation: Up to 50% of the balance at the end of the preceding financial year: 50% × ₹38,40,000 = ₹19,20,000. The rest keeps earning interest until maturity or closure on marriage.

children.text: SCSS is built for one job: turning a retirement corpus into a steady, government-backed quarterly income. The rate is fixed for the full 5 years on the day you invest, interest is paid on the first day of April, July, October and January, and deposits up to ₹1,50,000 in a year count under Section 123 (80C) on the old regime. It is available at post offices and authorised banks such as SBI, Bank of Baroda and ICICI Bank.

cards.definition: Anyone aged 60 or above. Also retirees aged 55 to 60 who invest within one month of receiving retirement benefits, and retired defence personnel aged 50 or above.
Only with your spouse. The entire deposit belongs to the first holder, and the ₹30 lakh limit applies to the first holder.
No interest is payable. Any interest already paid is recovered from the principal.

10% TDS if SCSS interest crosses ₹1,00,000 in a tax year. Submit Form 121 if your total income is below the taxable limit.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: The maximum an individual can invest across all SCSS accounts is ₹___ lakh.
body.explanation: The limit is ₹30 lakh per individual. A married couple, both eligible, can each open their own account and invest up to ₹60 lakh together, earning ₹1,23,000 every quarter at 8.2%.

body.text: SCSS interest is fully taxable. Only the deposit gets the 80C deduction, and only up to ₹1,50,000 even if you invest ₹30 lakh. On the old regime, senior citizens can also claim a deduction of up to ₹50,000 on interest from banks and post offices (80TTB under the 1961 Act), which covers part of the SCSS interest.

body.title: Scenario: The Retirement Corpus
body.scenario: Rajan, 62, a retired bank officer in Chennai, receives ₹45,00,000 in retirement benefits. He gets a pension of ₹40,000 a month. His wife Meenakshi, 60, is a homemaker with no income of her own. Rajan plans to put ₹30,00,000 in his SCSS account and ₹15,00,000 in a new SCSS account in Meenakshi's name 'to save tax, since her income is zero'.
body.prompt: Will this split save tax as Rajan expects? What should the couple watch out for?
body.modelAnswer: Not as he expects. The ₹15 lakh in Meenakshi's name comes from Rajan's retirement money, given to his spouse without adequate consideration. Under the clubbing provisions of the Income-tax Act, the ₹1,23,000 of interest earned on it is added to Rajan's income, not hers. The split still helps in two practical ways: it gets around the ₹30 lakh per-person limit so all ₹45 lakh can go into SCSS, and it gives Meenakshi her own account and income stream. Their total quarterly income is ₹61,500 + ₹30,750 = ₹92,250. On tax: only ₹1,50,000 of the deposit qualifies under 80C in total for Rajan. The banks or post office will deduct 10% TDS on each account where interest crosses ₹1 lakh in the year, and both accounts cross that line. Meenakshi should not submit Form 121 to stop TDS, since the income is taxable in Rajan's hands through clubbing. Rajan should report all SCSS interest in his return and claim credit for TDS deducted on both accounts. If Meenakshi had her own savings, from inheritance or earlier income, investing those in her SCSS account would genuinely shift the interest to her.

body.title: Before Opening SSY or SCSS
steps: SSY: confirm your daughter is below 10 and you have the birth certificate, your KYC and her Aadhaar ready
SSY: deposit early in the financial year, ideally between 1 and 5 April, to earn full interest
SSY: set a yearly reminder so the ₹250 minimum is never missed
SCSS: if aged 55 to 60, invest within one month of receiving retirement benefits
SCSS: invest only money you will not need for at least 2 years, to avoid penalties
SCSS: link a savings account so quarterly interest is credited automatically
Both: keep deposit receipts with your 80C proofs if you are on the old regime

points: SSY and SCSS both pay 8.2% for July to September 2026, the highest among government small savings schemes.
SSY is EEE: deposits qualify under Section 123 (80C) on the old regime, and interest and maturity are tax-free under both regimes.
SSY deposits run for 15 years and the account matures at 21 years, with 50% withdrawable for education from age 18.
SSY's rate changes quarterly; SCSS's rate is locked for 5 years on the day you invest.
SCSS pays interest every quarter on up to ₹30 lakh per person, but the interest is fully taxable.
Putting your own money into your spouse's SCSS account does not shift the tax: the interest is clubbed with your income.
